opus-5.5.text:
I think for me, the bar isn't a flashy demo — it's reliability in the boring sense. A first true version would be hardware you can actually leave running. Something that can operate for thousands of hours without a researcher standing next to it with a laptop and a screwdriver. Right now, a lot of robot hardware is still in a state where the mean time between failures is measured in days, sometimes hours, and that fundamentally limits how much data you can collect and how much you can learn.

Second, it has to be affordable enough to scale. If every unit costs as much as a car, you'll never get the fleet sizes needed to gather real-world data at the scale that learning-based methods want. So I'd say a first true version is something where the cost curve looks like consumer electronics rather than industrial equipment — maybe a few thousand dollars, not tens or hundreds of thousands.

Third, and this is the part people often underestimate, is the hand — or more generally, the interface with the world. Manipulation is where most of the value is, and today's grippers and hands are either too simple to do dexterous tasks or too fragile and complicated to survive daily use. A first true version needs a hand that's robust, has decent tactile sensing, and can handle the long tail of objects in a home or a factory without breaking itself.

And finally, safety. It has to be something you'd be comfortable having next to a person — compliant, lightweight enough, with low enough inertia that a mistake isn't dangerous. Because the real data, the real value, is in human environments.

So if you put those together — reliable, cheap, a capable and durable hand, and inherently safe — then I'd say, okay, that's version one. Everything before that, honestly, is still prototypes. We're getting closer, but I don't think we're fully there yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes reliable, affordable, safe hardware with a capable hand, but does not identify a home robot performing all desired household tasks under human remote control as the threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're not close yet, and the gap isn't where most people think it is.

When I say "first true version," I mean something like the iPhone moment. Not a demo, not a lab result, but a piece of hardware that you can hand to someone who has never seen it before, and it does something useful in their actual environment, reliably, for a long time, without an engineer standing next to it. By that standard, nothing exists today.

So what would it need? I'd break it into three things.

The first is reliability over time, not peak performance. Everyone shows the video where the robot folds the shirt perfectly. What I care about is: run it for a thousand hours. What's the failure rate? How many times does a human have to intervene? Today's humanoids are, frankly, prototypes that have to be rebuilt every few weeks. Motors overheat, cables fray, joints drift out of calibration. A first true version has to be boring. It has to work on Tuesday the same way it worked on Monday.

The second is the hand. I think the body gets too much attention and the hand gets too little. Walking is largely solved in a research sense. But a hand that can grasp an egg and also open a stuck jar, that has good touch sensing, that doesn't cost twenty thousand dollars and break in a month, that's still missing. Most useful work in the world happens through the hands. If the hand isn't there, the rest of the body is just an expensive way to move a bad hand around.

The third is cost at a level where the economics close. It doesn't have to be cheap, but it has to be cheaper than the labor it replaces over its lifetime, including maintenance. If you need a technician for every ten robots, you haven't really built a product, you've built a very complicated service business.

And I'd add one thing that people underestimate: the hardware has to be designed for the model, not the other way around. Right now a lot of teams build a body and then try to train a brain to control it. I think the first true version comes from a team that asks, what does the learning system actually need from the body? Maybe that means more sensors, simpler joints, more compliance, less precision. The body and the intelligence have to be co-designed.

So if you asked me for a single line: a first true version is hardware that a model can operate for a year in a real home or factory, doing one genuinely useful task, with less than one human intervention per day, at a cost that makes sense. When someone ships that, I'll call it version one.

r001.rationale: The response sets a threshold of a model reliably performing one useful task in a home or factory. It does not identify a home robot performing all desired household tasks under human remote control as sufficient.

astra-6.text: For me, the first true version would be a robot that can reliably do something useful in a real environment, without an engineer standing next to it. It doesn’t need to do everything. But if you give it a task, it should be able to complete it repeatedly, handle small changes, and stop safely when something goes wrong. The hardware also needs to be durable and affordable enough that someone actually wants to use it. That’s the threshold I’d care about: moving from an impressive demonstration to something you can depend on.

r001.rationale: The response describes reliably completing a useful task in a real environment without an engineer present, and explicitly says the robot need not do everything. It does not identify a home robot performing all desired household tasks under human remote control as the threshold.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the first true version would be a robot that can reliably complete a useful task from beginning to end in a real environment. It can’t just work once in a carefully prepared demo. It needs to repeat that task, handle small changes, and recover when something goes wrong without someone constantly stepping in.

So I’d look at the whole system: dexterity, sensing, power, durability, and cost. You don’t need human-level capability across everything. A narrow set of capabilities can be enough, provided the robot is dependable enough that someone actually wants to use it every day.

r001.rationale: The candidate sets the threshold at reliably completing a useful task and says a narrow set of capabilities can suffice. It does not identify performing all desired household tasks under human remote control as sufficient.
